newsitem.title: USA: BankAmerica reaches out to Calif. bond officials.
newsitem.headline: BankAmerica reaches out to Calif. bond officials.

text.p: BankAmerica Corp. is sending letters to more than 1,000 state and local government officials across California, admitting some mistakes in an embarrassing municipal bond scandal, but insisting they were unintentional.

In the letter, BankAmerica Chief Executive David Coulter said the bank discovered the billing errors on its own, calculated the amount of overcharge to each bond issuer and voluntarily made refunds totalling more than $5 million.
Coulter said the errors were "unintentional," adding that the bank "flatly rejects" allegations that it falsified records as part of a cover-up.

Both the city of San Francisco and the state of California have sued BankAmerica and its unit, Bank of America, for allegedly overcharging municipal bond issuers, failing to return unclaimed funds from bond accounts, and improperly investing some of the funds.
The state lawsuit claims hundreds of millions of dollars in damages. San Francisco is seeking more than $12 million.
The state's lawsuit arose out of the bank's role as trustee and paying agent on more than 10,000 bond issues involving over 1,000 state and local bond issuers.

More than $100 billion of bond funds were placed in state and local government accounts administered by the bank between 1978 and 1993, according to the state's lawsuit. The bank lost money in those accounts through "errors, mistakes, theft and poor management," the lawsuit alleged.
Coulter said the bank believes the refunds it has already paid out should cover the overcharges, but added, "we stand ready to pay any additional claims that can be substantiated."

"We take very seriously the issues raised in the recent lawsuits," Coulter said in his letter. "We have developed a reputation for integrity and reliability. So you can be sure that we will make every effort to see that any mistakes are resolved fairly and expeditiously."
Municipal bond analysts say the lawsuits could tarnish the bank's image in California, where its services are used by the vast majority of public agencies.
Some state and local government officials, however, are downplaying the dispute.
State finance officials said they do not believe the lawsuits will hurt the bank's relationship with most California agencies and authorities.
For its part, Los Angeles County, one of BankAmerica's largest municipal clients, says it remains committed to working with the bank despite the flap.

"For us, this is not a matter of concern," Los Angeles County Treasurer-Tax Collector Larry Monteilh said. "They're trying to do the right thing. I don't think the bank tried to pull the wool over anyone's eyes."
BankAmerica's stock fell $1.125 to $116.875 on the New York Stock Exchange.
